title: Bob Iger’s Translation of Thinking, Fast and Slow
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post borrows Daniel Kahneman's fast and slow thinking and shows how Disney's Bob Iger applied it as a matter of situation rather than psychology. Iger sorts most leadership decisions into crisis and strategy, and matches his thinking speed to each. In crisis he moved at once, as when he called the family of a child killed at a Disney resort within hours and took ownership of the response. In strategy, such as the Pixar, Marvel and Lucasfilm acquisitions, he spent years assessing cultures, building trust and bringing the board along. The author's conclusion is that the skill is diagnosis, not speed: leaders falter when they default to one speed regardless of the problem.
points: Iger's framework divides leadership decisions into crisis, which demands fast action and ownership, and strategy, which demands deliberate buy-in.
The Lane Graves phone call is a concrete example of fast thinking: immediate, personal and accepting responsibility.
The Pixar, Marvel and Lucasfilm deals illustrate slow thinking driven by the size of the bet and the need to build trust.
Leaders fail when they apply a single speed to every situation.
The real discipline is diagnosing what kind of problem you face before choosing how fast to think.
quotes: In Thinking, Fast and Slow, the renowned behavioral economist Daniel Kahneman argued that most thinking is driven by a fast, intuitive mental system that is remarkably efficient but prone to predictable biases. Slower, more deliberate thinking can improve judgment when people consciously engage it.

Iger believes good leaders match their thinking to the size and shape of the problem, and that most leadership decisions sort into two categories: crisis and strategy. In Iger’s view, crisis requires leaders to communicate quickly, show up immediately, and take responsibility swiftly. This is fast thinking.

Iger was in Shanghai for the opening of Disney’s new park there, but he called the boy’s family within hours. Iger wanted them to hear from him personally. He took full ownership of the company’s response to the tragedy.

He methodically assessed the companies’ cultures and built trust with the people who would have to say yes. He brought his board along step by step before betting billions on decisions that would define Disney for a generation.
The two demands pull in opposite directions. Crisis rewards leaders who are willing to move before every fact is known.

Iger’s genius wasn’t in being fast, or in being slow, but in knowing which clock he was on. A burning building doesn’t wait for a steering committee, and a large acquisition doesn’t reward a coin flip.
Iger’s real lesson isn’t found in Kahneman’s work at all. It’s a discipline of diagnosis. First ask what kind of problem you are facing.
